claims.text: The studied material is equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn is single-phase and primarily FCC.
The initial FeNiCrMn material has a relatively low defect density.
The dynamic mechanical response of FeNiCrMn is governed by competition between thermally activated dislocation slip and mechanically activated deformation twinning.
Low temperatures and high strain rates limit thermal activation and suppress dislocation cross-slip and recovery.
Suppressed dislocation mobility at low temperatures and high strain rates favors twin nucleation and makes twinning the dominant strain-hardening mechanism.
Deformation twinning enhances work hardening and strength and delays strain localization or failure.
Higher temperatures and lower strain rates increase dislocation glide and cross-slip and facilitate dynamic recovery.
Dynamic recovery at higher temperatures or lower strain rates reduces flow stress while preserving ductility.
The twin fraction will increase under low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading relative to quasi-static baseline conditions.
Flow stress and strain-hardening rate will vary nonlinearly with temperature and strain rate.
At high temperatures and low strain rates, dislocation slip and recovery will predominate, producing lower flow stress but sustained ductility.
Under quasi-static loading at moderate temperatures, conventional dislocation slip governs plasticity and twinning is limited.
The mechanism is intended to apply only to single-phase Co-free FeNiCrMn with minimal secondary phases and low impurity levels.
Significant pre-existing defects, coarse grains, or additive elements that change stacking-fault energy may cause deviations from the proposed mechanism.
Trends in related high-entropy alloy systems support competition between twinning and dislocation slip.
The transition temperatures and strain rates are not yet determined and may depend on processing history and microstructural features.
The proposed test matrix spans 200–800 K and strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Twin volume fraction, dislocation density, flow stress, and strain-hardening rate will be measured as functions of temperature and strain rate.
